items.title: Why Your Shoes Come Untied
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Why do your shoes laces keep untying themselves? It could be because you're out there running all the time, which vibrates your shoes until the knot loosens. Yeah, that's not the case for most of us. It could be because you're tying them wrong. We are supposed to use a reef knot, a term I'd never heard, essentially a square knot with loops for easy untying. Yet some people tie a granny knot, which doesn't hold well at all. There are other knots that people swear by, but you have to have the motivation to learn them. Kids' shoes come untied all the time because they are so active and inattentive, so I used to double tie my kids' shoes or use those plastic clips to keep the knot in place. 

My feet are small, so I buy shoes from the kids' section because they cost less. My current tennis shoes are tied, then have a velcro strap that closes right over the knot, so no worries. If you need some help keeping your shoes tied, astrophysicist Josie Peters has the science of shoelaces to help you out. (via

Laughing Squid)

items.title: The Atlantic Ocean is Acting Weird
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
We've heard of the Gulf Stream, but it's just a part of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC). AMOC flows one way on the surface, and then a different direction in the lower depths of the ocean. This explains why the coldest regions of the continental US are at the same latitudes as the warmest parts of Europe. We will also be introduced to the "cold blob" in the ocean. But this system has shown some changes lately, thanks to glacial melting in Greenland. What does that mean for us?

The effects would be felt in Europe first, but it may affect other parts of the world as well. When will all this happen? Scientists are leery of assigning a date to the point of no return, or the point of environmental collapse. Other factors may be in play, and we can't say that today's trajectory will not change. Still, ocean currents that have been stable for a few thousand years suddenly starting to change can't be a good thing.

items.title: Is It Too Early To Decorate For Christmas?
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
When I was a kid, my parents would pull out the Christmas decorations after Thanksgiving. When I had kids, we'd gradually start decorating when they started asking about it, which was right after Halloween. After they left home, I always made it a point to have the outdoor Christmas lights up to greet my Thanksgiving guests (we usually have the feast at suppertime). I ask my kids to put up the tree and the ornaments when they are here for Thanksgiving. 

I get a kick out of noticing how my neighbors do it. Some just replace Halloween decor with Christmas, either on November first or sometime in December when the skeletons get really dirty. Some even

combine the two holidays on their lawn. I don't decorate for Halloween anymore. 

This year, Princess can't come because of her husband's work schedule, and Dr. Dolittle only has one day off, so she and her husband won't have time to help decorate. I guess I better get started on the house prep. I have to move furniture to get the tree up, and I want to mop the floor in between. Hauling heavy stuff from the basement has to be done a little at a time, and during daylight. Outside lights take a couple of days because there are few hours that are warm enough. The logistics get harder every year, but it's still a lot of fun. And it gives me an excuse for not raking leaves until December.

items.title: Hi
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The entire YouTube description for the latest video from Bill Wurtz (previously at Neatorama) is "oops, no ai". What's the story? There is none. This is just following a guy around as he moves through his day, constantly distracted by something else and accomplishing very little along the way. He does get his roof done, but the actual work was done by someone else. 

a song? No, but there are musical elements to it here and there. The real genius is in two-second snippets of philosophical thoughts that only make sense when they are taken out of context. The context is a nonsensical framework that seems to be built only to get from one snippet to the next. Or perhaps I am overthinking it. This is probably better enjoyed as the surreal stream of consciousness that it appears to be on the surface. Oh yeah, and there's the Infinity Bus.

items.title: State Borders Are Hard to Draw From Memory
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:

Drawing each state's borders is not easy when you've never done it before, no matter how well you know the US map. Some people are astonishingly good at it. Then you remember that no one is going to try the game unless they think they can do it. 

A compilation map of how all players drew those lines is fascinating.

Matt Forrest brings us some insights about that map, specifically that the states with the most complicated borders turn out to be the easiest states to place. The hardest are those with simple, straight borders because they are all together in the American West. (via Laughing Squid)

items.title: The Dying Minutes of World War One
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Canadian soldier George Lawrence Price, from Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan, was serving with the 28th Infantry Battalion on November 11. The 26-year-old was part of a five-man patrol that was checking buildings beside the canal at Ville-sur-Haine, in Mons, for signs of the enemy.

Unfortunately, they found them – a group of German soldiers in the process of setting up machine guns on a wall overlooking the canal. There was an exchange of fire; both sides took cover and the Germans retreated.

The Canadians began to follow, but just as George stepped out onto the street he was shot in the chest by a German sniper. Dragged into a nearby house, he was treated by a local nurse, but there was little she could do.

George Price died soon after, at 10.58am… just two minutes before the armistice.

items.title: Five Species That Harness Wildfires
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
For most animals, plants, and other life forms, fire is the worst thing that can happen. It's deadly, and even if you escape, your environment is ruined. But wildfires have always been a part of earth's activities, and some species have evolved to use it to their benefit. For example, the fire lily bulb stays dormant in the ground until after a wildfire rages through. Then it grows and blooms without competition from other plants!  

Plants that grow in the ashes of a wildfire attracts bugs, which attract birds. It's almost as if there's a system to heal and renew the environment after its devastated by fire. There are other species that are attracted to wildfires, and even one that actively spreads a fire. SciScow introduces us to how all this works. This video has a skippable ad from 6:00 to 6:48.

items.title: The History of Salt
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content: We all need salt to function, so animals evolved to seek it out. Lucky for us, the salty seas have left deposits of salt everywhere, if we can find them. Humans, however, sought salt so much that today our doctors tell us to lay off the salty snacks and put away the shaker because it can lead to high blood pressure. It wasn't always this way, because salt was not always so easy to get. the quest for salt as a commodity goes all the way back to the beginning of agriculture. Those who had it became rich selling it, although it wasn't easy- that's why working in the salt mines became a metaphor for backbreaking, unpleasant labor. Getting salt to those who had less became one of the reasons we developed global trade. This TED-Ed lesson brings us a short history of sale, but try to resist the urge to grab some chips while watching it.

items.title: Atomic Chicken

Then one day something goes wrong, and the farm is showered with radioactive fallout. The effects are the ridiculous extremes we saw in 1950s B-movies, like immediate mutant growth and unexplainable super powers. The chickens are still birdbrains, but they have an idea of how to stop the  nuclear plant from contaminating their environment. 

Atomic Chicken is a student film from the French art school Ecole des Nouvelles, specifically the 2023 graduation film for animation students. I like the animated fabric textures, but was a little surprised at one point. "Hey, we can see this chicken's cloaca!" There's a reason for that, since a hen's main talent is laying eggs, and that's important to the story, although what they do with that talent is surprising. (via

items.title: Star Wars Copies From the 1970s

came out in 1977, it was an immediate monster hit. Filmmakers everywhere, but especially in Italy, sat up and noticed. If the audience wants a space Western, that's what they'll get! But we had already seen space adventures for many years, so what was it about that people loved so much? A series of movies were churned out that tried to emulate as best they could, going so far as to rip off character designs and plot lines from a galaxy far, far away. The most famous of these knockoffs was an Italian film with movie stars and space battles, but not much else.

items.title: Yes, 42 is a Special Number
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Yeah, you saw the question in the title and said, "That's the answer to life, the universe, and everything!" And you are right; that was the premise of Douglas' Adams story The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. But also remember, by the time the supercomputer once known as earth rendered the answer, it occurred to everyone that they no longer knew what the question was. The real question for Adams was, why 42? There was nothing special about that number, he assured us. But is that true? The number 42 crops up in plenty of ancients texts and classic literature. Could these have influenced Adams? And what if they didn't? The number is certainly important now, thanks to The Hitchhiker's Guide.

items.title: Portuguese Man O' War
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The Portuguese man o' war is not from Portugal, and it's neither a man nor at war. but more importantly, it's not a jellyfish, either, although it looks like one. This creature cannot even propel itself through the water, and relies on ocean currents to move at all. As such, you'd think they would stay in their own ecosystem. But climate change is bringing warm waters to more places than ever before, and the man o' war is spreading with those waters. Why is this important?

For one, we don't know what effect they will have as an invasive species, and how the man o' war will upset the balance of nature. The other reason is closer to home- they can kill humans. A Portuguese man o' war's sting can range from painful and bothersome to lethal, with all kinds of unpleasant effects in between that can last up to a year. You don't want to mess with these animals, even when they are stranded on the beach. Even though they are pretty.

items.title: The Most Hated "Americanisms"
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Commenter William Rocket constantly complains about the way Americans use English. We mostly ignore him, because we all know British English and American English are just different, and that's okay. Laurence Brown of Lost in the Pond has spent years humorously explaining the differences between the two cultures. Over those years he's become more and more American (he's a US citizen now) while keeping his British accent. We can see that in how he defends what are known as "Americanisms." Well, they are known as Americanisms outside of America. I had no idea these words and phrases were unique to the US. 

With some research, Brown has determined that Americanisms from a BBC complaint list either originated in Britain or are perfectly understandable in context or are just plain correct. I agree with him that "normalcy" is not a word, but I'm not inclined to argue about it. This video has a skippable ad from 4:24 to 5:57.

items.title: Hyperburn
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Hyperburn is a new science fiction short from DUST that's a post-apocalyptic battle scene and somewhat of a comedy, too. Our protagonist appears to be from a ragtag rebel group fighting against an oppressive regime with spaceships. He becomes stranded in the desert alone when his transportation equipment is damaged. That kind of scene is always a problem for filmmakers because of the lack of dialogue. But this guy has had an artificial intelligence agent implanted in his brain, so that's someone to talk to. She knows more about what's going on in his body than he really wants to hear, up to a point. Is she smarter than he is, or is she just a nag? 

Travis DuBridge made Hyperburn, a two-year project which he wrote, storyboarded, rehearsed, and made all the props and costumes. Yes, he had a small cast and crew when it came time to film. DuBridge laid out all the concepts and behind-the-scenes explainers at his channel. (via Geeks Are Sexy)

I had one that we thought was a tortoiseshell, but she must have been a calico underneath because she was psychotic. Right now I have a white cat, gray cat, tabby, and a calico. Two are seniors. They all display the exact qualities here. Apollo was the epitome of an orange cat. Disappointed there are no color point cats in this graph.

items.title: The Brain That Wouldn't Die
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
This movie scared me something awful when I was a little kid. It was released in 1962. From Wikipedia:
The Brain That Wouldn't Die (also known as The Head That Wouldn't Die) is a 1962 American science fiction horror film directed by Joseph Green and written by Green and Rex Carlton.[1] The film was completed in 1959 under the working title The Black Door but was not theatrically released until May 3, 1962, when it was released under its renamed title on a double bill with Invasion of the Star Creatures.[2][3]
The main plot focuses upon a mad doctor who develops a means to keep human body parts alive. He keeps a woman's severed head alive for days, and keeps a lumbering, misshapened brute (one of his earlier failed experiments) imprisoned in a closet.

items.title: Rockin' in the Rockies
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The 1945 movie Rockin' in the Rockies is the Three Stooges' first feature length movie, despite the fact that it isn't all that much longer than their series of shorts. It is the only lone of their feature films to star Curly Howard. Don't mistake Rockin' in the Rockies with an earlier Three Stooges short titled Rockin' Through the Rockies. In this movie, the Stooges travel to a Nevada ranch to supervise it temporarily, and are accompanied by two ladies who are singers wanting to make it big and get their chance at a Reno casino. So it's a Western musical comedy. (Thanks, WTM!)

items.title: The Godawan
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Godawan whisky is an ecologically sustainable whisky company in India that was named after the critically-endangered godawan, or great Indian bustard. The distillery has worked for 20 years to save the species. Godawan teamed up with Studio Eeksaurus to produce a video about the bird. The song that narrates the story is in the Rajasthani dialect, so you'll want to make sure the closed captions are on and in English.    

For this animation, they used 5200 separate ceramic pieces, many custom-made, inspired by the blue pottery of Jaipur. A hundred people spent 15,000 hours creating the film. At about 4:40, we get a behind the scenes look at how the film was made. You can read more about the project in an interview with the director.  (via Metafilter)
